[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Python Classes and Objects: A Comprehensive Guide"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Python is an object-oriented programming language. Almost everything in Python is an object, with its properties and methods. A class is like a blueprint for creating objects."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Defining a Class"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"To create a class, use the keyword 'class':"},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"class MyClass:
  x = 5"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Creating an Object"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Now we can use the class named MyClass to create objects:"},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"p1 = MyClass()
print(p1.x)"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"The __init__() Function"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"The __init__() function is a special method that is called when the object is being created. It is used to initialize the object's attributes."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"class Person:
  def __init__(self, name, age):
    self.name = name
    self.age = age

p1 = Person("John", 36)

print(p1.name)
print(p1.age)"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Object Methods"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Objects can also contain methods. Methods are functions that belong to the object."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"class Person:
  def __init__(self, name, age):
    self.name = name
    self.age = age

  def myfunc(self):
    print("Hello my name is " + self.name)

p1 = Person("John", 36)
p1.myfunc()"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"The 'self' Parameter"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"The 'self' parameter is a reference to the current instance of the class, and is used to access variables that belong to the class."},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"It does not have to be named 'self' , you can call it whatever you like, but it has to be the first parameter of any function in the class:"},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"class Person:
  def __init__(mysillyobject, name, age):
    mysillyobject.name = name
    mysillyobject.age = age

  def myfunc(abc):
    print("Hello my name is " + abc.name)

p1 = Person("John", 36)
p1.myfunc()"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Modifying Object Properties"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can modify properties of an object:"},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"p1.age = 40

print(p1.age)"},{"order":22,"type":"subheading","text":"Deleting Object Properties"},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can delete properties of an object by using the 'del' keyword:"},{"order":24,"type":"code","text":"del p1.age"},{"order":25,"type":"subheading","text":"Deleting Objects"},{"order":26,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can delete objects by using the 'del' keyword:"},{"order":27,"type":"code","text":"del p1"},{"order":28,"type":"subheading","text":"Pass Statement"},{"order":29,"type":"paragraph","text":"class definitions cannot be empty, but if you for some reason have a class definition with no content, put in the 'pass' statement to avoid getting an error."},{"order":30,"type":"code","text":"class Person:
  pass"}]
